s01.title: Beneath the ground
s01.short: Long before any estate paper, Llandough was lived on: a Roman villa, an early Christian cemetery of over a thousand burials beside the church, and finds later lost in a 1983 fire.

s02.title: The name Cedwyn
s02.short: The name Cedwyn runs through the land: Cwm-Cedwyn on the Ely, Nant-Cedwyn, Cwm Cydfin Wood. Our reading: the name is older than the estate papers.

s03.title: Tŷ Mawr on the map
s03.short: 1824: a survey draws the holding as plan 19, Cedfin or Tŷ Mawr Farm, with a table of its fields. The first mention found so far in the estate surveys.

s04.title: The tithe map
s04.short: About 1841: the tithe list puts John Williams on 36 parcels, 33 entered against Bute. A tithe list did not test title; our reading is that this Bute entry is the one to scrutinise.

s05.title: Rates and the quarry
s05.short: 1872 to 1877: rate books name John Williams; an 1877 Bute agreement with a quarry firm touches the house parcel. Our reading: the start of the limeworks carve-up.

s06.title: A household of standing
s06.short: 1881 to 1910: John Williams, farmer, in the census; on the court leet grand jury in 1910. Our reading: a family of standing in the parish.

s07.title: Woods, drains and estate papers
s07.short: 1902 to 1931: estate auctions, conveyances and a 1916 estate paper the family contest. Meanwhile the family plant trees, the native custom of asserting ownership.

s08.title: Transferred over their heads
s08.short: 1938 to 1942: the Bute interest passes to Western Ground Rents; a 1939 paper is drawn up in John Williams's name. Our reading: the land changed hands on paper without the family.

s09.title: The courts begin
s09.short: 1949 to 1957: an unwritten re-grant, title papers missing from the farmhouse, then the county court. Our reading: occupation recast as permission.

s10.title: A Welsh Crichel Down
s10.short: 1958: Mrs Mary Buckler of Tŷ Mawr calls it a Welsh Crichel Down: land farmed by her family since 1667, wrongfully appropriated.

s11.title: Orders, a school and a green
s11.short: 1959 to 1970: offers, a 1962 order, the school site in 1965, BP in 1969, and parcel C registered as village green in 1970. Our reading: taken a parcel at a time.

s12.title: The survey and the open day
s12.short: 1974: the Royal Commission measures the house; an open day to save it; Mary Williams pleads ownership. 1975: the house moves between BP companies on paper.

s13.title: Registered
s13.short: 1982 to 1983: the land, then the farmhouse, first registered as titles WA231076 and WA240304. Our reading: the registration step in the pattern.

s14.title: Judgment
s14.short: 1986 to 1987: High Court, then Court of Appeal, for BP. The local plan still marked the buildings to be retained.

s15.title: The house comes down
s15.short: 1988: eviction, then on 7 December bulldozers just after 4 am. By breakfast nothing stood, while listing was still being considered.

s16.title: After
s16.short: 1989 to 1996: building destroyed by owners, the record notes. Houses and a green follow; the 1994 dig finds the early Christian cemetery.

s17.title: In the law books
s17.short: 2002 onward: the case becomes a textbook lesson on adverse possession while the land passes on.

s18.title: Asking the record holders
s18.short: 2026: the record holders are asked directly. Every answer becomes a catalogue entry; every gap a missing record.

p1.title: The barn
p1.text: Location one: the barn. At Tŷ Mawr the barn stood across the yard from the house, and it was the ground for parish life. A photograph in the People's Collection Wales shows a chapel fete at Great House Farm, with the barn behind the crowd, a slide for the children and a refreshment tent. Testimony holds that Peerless Jim Driscoll, the Cardiff boxing champion, fought one of his early bouts in this barn, and that a Welsh roundhouse was found beneath it. Neither is yet in the evidence catalogue. What the catalogue does hold: Cadw photographed this barn on 29 July 1988, months before it was pulled down, and the ground around it carried a Roman villa and an early Christian cemetery.

p2.title: The main house
p2.text: Location two: the main house, Tŷ Mawr, the former manorial house of Llandough. In 1824 a survey draws it as Cedfin or Tŷ Mawr Farm, plan 19. In 1881 the census finds John Williams and his household here, and in 1910 he sits on the grand jury of the court leet. In 1958 Mary Doreen Buckler, speaking from this house, calls the loss of the family's land since 1667 a Welsh Crichel Down. In April 1974 the Royal Commission measures every room, the drawing this replica is built from, and the house holds an open day to save it. In 1982 and 1983 the land and the house are first registered to others. In December 1988 bulldozers arrive just after four in the morning, while listing is still under consideration. Our reading: the house is the centre of the whole chronology, and it stands again here.

p3.title: The church
p3.text: Location three: the church. St Dochdwy's stood a few steps from the house. The 1994 excavation north of the church recorded more than a thousand early Christian burials, and Cadw listed the church in 1989. The church of the seventeenth century will not be rebuilt in Patagonia, so it appears here as a hologram. No image of that medieval church has been found yet: this hologram is traced from the oldest photograph found, of the church that stood here before 1866.

p4.title: The yard and the stables
p4.text: Location four: the yard and the stables, the working heart of the farm. Parish books of the 1870s name John Williams here, and in 1891 a newspaper reports three geese taken from his yard. The family planted trees on the land, the native custom of asserting ownership, and a family photograph records it. From 1916 the estate side drew up papers describing the family's occupation on its own terms; the family contest every one of them. Around 1950 the family's title papers went missing from the blanket box in the house, and the county court registers open in 1953. Our reading: each paper recast a long occupation as permission.

p5.title: The gate and the green
p5.text: Location five: the entrance gate, looking out to what was parcel C. In 1965 land of the estate went for the Llandough school, and in June 1970 parcel C was registered as village green VG41. After 1988 the site became a housing plan, with a village green planting scheme. In 2026 the record holders were asked directly: the Land Registry, Cadw, the archives. Every answer is a catalogue entry; every gap is a missing record. Our reading: the gate is where the estate went out, parcel by parcel, and where the record now comes back in.
